verses.context: The crossing ordered in 4:35 ends on the eastern shore, in Gentile country. The storm on the lake is followed at once by a storm in a man, and the story shows the same authority at work: the one who silenced the sea now silences a legion.
verses.grammar: Eis to peran tēs thalassēs, ‘to the other side of the sea’, picks up 4:35 exactly. Eis tēn chōran tōn Gerasēnōn, ‘into the region of the Gerasenes’, names a territory (chōra), not a town, a distinction that matters for the geographical problem described below.
verses.text: The manuscripts of all three Gospels disagree about the name, and scribes plainly tried to solve a geographical difficulty. In Mark the earliest witnesses (Codex Sinaiticus in its original hand, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and the Latin tradition) read ‘Gerasenes’. Codex Alexandrinus and the great majority of later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Gadarenes’. A corrector of Sinaiticus and several other manuscripts, including Codex Regius (L) and the Koridethi Gospels (Θ), read ‘Gergesenes’. The best text of Luke (8:26, 37) also reads Gerasenes, while the best text of Matthew (8:28) reads Gadarenes, and Matthew tells of two men rather than one.
verses.history: Each name points to a real place. Gerasa, modern Jerash in Jordan, was a prosperous city of the Decapolis more than 50 kilometers (over 30 miles) southeast of the lake, too far for a herd to stampede into the water. Gadara, modern Umm Qais, lay about 10 kilometers (6 miles) southeast of the lake above the Yarmuk gorge, and its territory probably reached the shore, which suits Matthew's reading. In the third century Origen (Commentary on John, book 6) rejected both: Gerasa, he said, was a town of Arabia with no sea or lake near it, and Gadara had famous hot springs but no lake with overhanging banks. He preferred Gergesa, an old town beside the lake with a steep slope pointed out as the place where the swine were cast down. In 1970 road builders on the eastern shore uncovered the remains at Kursi, where Vassilios Tzaferis excavated a large Byzantine monastery and church and, up the slope, a small chapel built around a rock, evidently marking the traditional site of the miracle. Many scholars think Kursi preserves the name Gergesa. Mark's ‘region of the Gerasenes’ may simply use the best-known city's name for the whole district, as a writer from outside Palestine might.

verses.context: The moment Jesus steps from the boat he is met by a man from the tombs. Mark introduces him with the same phrase he used for the man in the Capernaum synagogue (1:23), "a man with an unclean spirit", so the first exorcism on Gentile soil mirrors the first on Jewish soil.
verses.grammar: Exelthontos autou ek tou ploiou, ‘when he had come out of the boat’, is a genitive absolute, and then autō, ‘him’, follows in the dative for the same person. Classical Greek avoided this, but Mark's everyday Greek often does it. Euthus hupēntēsen autō, ‘immediately he met him’: the man comes to Jesus, not the reverse. Anthrōpos en pneumati akathartō, literally ‘a man in an unclean spirit’, uses en in the sense of the Hebrew preposition be, ‘with’ or ‘under the power of’; the man is inside the spirit's control as much as the spirit is inside him. Ek tōn mnēmeiōn, ‘from the tombs’, uses the word for a memorial tomb.

ot.note: Isaiah 65:1-7 describes a rebellious people who provoke God to his face, "sitting among the graves, spending nights in secret places, eating the meat of pigs". The Septuagint sharpens the picture: they burn incense ‘to demons (daimoniois), which do not exist’, and ‘sleep in the tombs (en tois mnēmasin) and in the caves for the sake of dreams’. Mark does not quote the passage, but his scene gathers nearly all its elements: tombs (the same word, mnēmasin, in verses 3 and 5), demons, pigs, and a people far from God. Joel Marcus and others have suggested that Mark's hearers were meant to recognize the picture of uncleanness from Isaiah and to see Jesus entering it. Paul quotes the opening of the same chapter, God found by those who did not seek him, of the Gentiles (Romans 10:20).

verses.text: Matthew has two men, not one, and describes them as so violent that no one could pass that way (8:28); Luke says the man was from the town and had not worn clothes for a long time (8:27). Matthew also has two blind men where Mark has one (Matthew 20:30), and interpreters have long suggested that Matthew knew of a second person whom Mark's more focused story leaves aside, or that he doubles witnesses in keeping with the law's requirement of two (Deuteronomy 19:15).

verses.context: Mark gives the man's condition at unusual length, in a sequence that the end of the story will reverse point by point. He lives among the dead, cannot be bound, has broken every chain, cannot be tamed, and cries out and cuts himself night and day. Every human attempt to control him has failed.
verses.grammar: Verse 3 piles up negatives: oude halusei ouketi oudeis edunato auton dēsai, literally ‘not even with a chain no longer no one was able to bind him’. Greek, unlike English, uses stacked negatives to strengthen rather than cancel each other. Verse 4 gives the reason with dia and three perfect passive infinitives, dedesthai, diespasthai, suntetriphthai: he ‘had been bound’, the chains ‘had been torn apart’, the shackles ‘had been smashed’. Oudeis ischuen auton damasai, ‘no one had the strength to tame him’, uses damazō, the verb for taming a wild animal (James 3:7-8), and ischuō, which recalls the ‘strong man’ (ischuros) of 3:27, who can be bound only by someone stronger. In verse 5 ēn krazōn kai katakoptōn, ‘he was crying out and cutting’, is a periphrastic imperfect, describing a way of life.
verses.history: Rock-cut tombs and burial caves lined the hillsides around the lake's eastern shore, and in Jewish law contact with a corpse, a bone, or a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11-16). To live among tombs was to live permanently in the place of death and defilement. The chains and fetters show that the local community had tried to restrain him, perhaps to protect others and perhaps him from himself, without success.

theology.note: The description is of a human life being unmade: cut off from community, living among the dead, unable to rest, harming his own body. The verses show what evil does to the image of God in a person, and they prepare for a rescue that restores all of it.

verses.context: The man runs to Jesus and falls before him, but the voice that speaks is the spirit's. It knows Jesus' identity, tries to hold him off with an oath, and begs not to be tormented. Verse 8 explains, after the fact, that Jesus had already commanded the spirit to come out; the story is told out of order to put the spirit's cry first.
verses.grammar: Prosekunēsen, ‘he bowed down’, can describe worship or simply prostration before a superior; here it is the posture of a defeated power. Ti emoi kai soi, literally ‘what to me and to you?’, is a Hebrew idiom (mah li walakh) meaning ‘what do we have to do with each other?’, used to push someone away (Judges 11:12, 1 Kings 17:18, Mark 1:24). Horkizō se ton theon, ‘I adjure you by God’, is the language of exorcism itself: an exorcist put a spirit under oath by a divine name. The spirit tries to exorcise Jesus. Mē me basanisēs, ‘do not torment me’, uses basanizō, torture or torment, which in Jewish and Christian writing is the fate of evil powers at the judgment (Revelation 20:10). Elegen gar, ‘for he had been saying’, an imperfect with gar, gives the explanation after the scene, a common Markan move (compare 6:17-18).
verses.history: ‘Most High God’ (theos hupsistos) was a title of Israel's God that Gentiles used and that Jews used when speaking to Gentiles: Melchizedek, the Canaanite priest-king, blesses Abram by God Most High (Genesis 14:18-20), Nebuchadnezzar calls the three Hebrews servants of the Most High God (Daniel 3:26), and a slave girl in Philippi uses the same title (Acts 16:17). The oath formula has close parallels in the Greek magical papyri, where spells adjure spirits by the names of gods; one spell in the great Paris papyrus (PGM IV.3019) even adjures a spirit by the god of the Hebrews, Jesus. Acts 19:13 describes Jewish exorcists in Ephesus adjuring spirits by Jesus' name.
verses.text: Matthew's demoniacs ask whether Jesus has come to torment them ‘before the time’ (8:29), making explicit that the demons know of an appointed judgment. Luke says the man had often been seized and kept under guard (8:29).

theology.note: The demons know who Jesus is before any human being in Mark says so. They call him Son of the Most High God and expect him to judge them. Their knowledge is accurate and useless: it is recognition without trust (compare James 2:19).

verses.context: Jesus asks the name, and the answer reveals a multitude: Legion. The spirit then begs not to be sent out of the region. The exchange shows who is in control: the spirits negotiate, but only for terms of their defeat.
verses.grammar: The grammar of the answer shows the man's condition. Legei autō, ‘he says to him’, is singular, and so is onoma moi, ‘my name’; then comes hoti polloi esmen, ‘because we are many’, plural. One voice speaks for many. Legiōn is a Latin loanword (legio) written in Greek letters. In verse 10 parekalei auton polla, ‘he kept begging him earnestly’, is an imperfect with polla used as an adverb. The spirits ask not to be sent exō tēs chōras, ‘out of the region’.
verses.history: A Roman legion in the first century numbered roughly five thousand infantry with a small cavalry detachment. The word is one of several Latin terms in Mark's Greek, alongside spekoulatōr, ‘executioner’ (6:27), dēnarion (6:37), kodrantēs, a small Roman coin (12:42), praitōrion (15:16), and kenturiōn (15:39). These Latinisms are often cited in support of the early tradition that Mark wrote in Rome, though others point out that such military and commercial terms were common throughout the eastern provinces. In the ancient world, knowing a spirit's name was thought to give power over it, but Jesus does not use the name to perform the exorcism; he already had authority (verse 8).
verses.text: Luke says the demons begged not to be sent ‘into the Abyss’ (8:31), the place of confinement for evil powers (Revelation 9:1-2, 20:1-3); Mark's ‘out of the region’ is more local and may reflect the belief that spirits were attached to particular places.

theology.note: The spirits are many and organized, yet they cannot act without Jesus' permission. The verses picture evil as real and powerful but wholly subject to him.

verses.context: A great herd of pigs is feeding on the hillside. The spirits ask to be sent into them, Jesus permits it, and the whole herd, about two thousand, rushes down the slope into the sea and drowns. The destruction makes visible what the man had endured and shows that the spirits have truly left him.
verses.grammar: Pempson hēmas eis tous choirous, ‘send us into the pigs’, is an aorist imperative, blunt after the pleading of verse 10. Epetrepsen autois, ‘he permitted them’, is a single word, and it is the only thing Jesus does in the whole transaction. Hōrmēsen hē agelē kata tou krēmnou, ‘the herd rushed down the steep bank’: hormaō describes a charge or stampede. Epnigonto, ‘they were drowning’, is an imperfect, picturing the herd going under animal by animal. Hōs dischilioi, ‘about two thousand’, is placed awkwardly in the Greek, almost as an afterthought.
verses.history: Pigs were forbidden food under the law (Leviticus 11:7, Deuteronomy 14:8), and in Jewish memory they carried a heavier charge: the Seleucid king Antiochus IV ordered pigs sacrificed and eaten as part of his attempt to abolish Judaism in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:47), and 2 Maccabees 6:18 to 7:42 tells of the scribe Eleazar and a mother and her seven sons who died rather than eat pork. For a Jewish hearer a herd of two thousand pigs marked this as thoroughly Gentile ground. J. D. M. Derrett suggested that the drowning in the sea was meant to recall Pharaoh's army sinking in the sea at the exodus (Exodus 15:4-5). Augustine used the story against the Manichaeans, who forbade killing animals, arguing that Christ showed by it that human beings do not share a common moral community with beasts (On the Morals of the Manichaeans 2.17).
verses.text: Only Mark gives the number of pigs. Matthew says the whole herd rushed down and died in the waters (8:32); Luke says it rushed into the lake (8:33), using limnē, his word for the Sea of Galilee.

theology.note: The demons are allowed to go where they ask, and what they enter they destroy. The verse shows the character of evil: it does not merely occupy but ruins, and it has no life of its own apart from what it can possess.

verses.context: The herdsmen flee and spread the news in town and country, and people come to see. What they find is the reversal of verses 3 to 5: the man who could not be restrained is sitting, the man among the tombs is clothed, the man who cried out and cut himself is in his right mind. And they are afraid.
verses.grammar: Erchontai and theōrousin, ‘they come’ and ‘they see’, are historic presents that put the reader among the crowd. The man is described with three participles, kathēmenon, himatismenon, sōphronounta, ‘sitting, clothed, and of sound mind’. Sōphroneō means to be of sound mind, self-controlled, the opposite of the madness just described; Paul uses it of sober judgment (Romans 12:3). Ton eschēkota ton legiōna, ‘the one who had had the legion’, uses a perfect participle to name the man by what he had been. Mark had not said the man was naked; ‘clothed’ implies it, and Luke says it outright (8:27). Ephobēthēsan, ‘they were afraid’, is the verb used of the disciples after the storm (4:41): both miracles end in fear at Jesus.

theology.note: The rescue is complete: mind, body, clothing, and a place in the world are all restored. Luke adds that the man was sitting at Jesus' feet (8:35), the posture of a disciple. Salvation in the Gospels is never only inward.

verses.context: The eyewitnesses tell what happened both to the man and to the pigs, and the people respond by begging Jesus to leave. The townspeople weigh the man's healing against the loss of the herd and the disturbing power that caused both, and they choose to be rid of Jesus.
verses.grammar: Diēgēsanto, ‘they described in detail’, and pōs egeneto, ‘how it happened’, show a full account. Kai peri tōn choirōn, ‘and about the pigs’, is added last, as though that was the part that decided the matter. Ērxanto parakalein auton, ‘they began to beg him’, is the fourth use of parakaleō, ‘beg’, in the story: the spirits begged not to be sent away (verse 10) and to be sent into the pigs (verse 12), the townspeople beg Jesus to leave (verse 17), and the healed man will beg to go with him (verse 18). The same verb traces who wants what from Jesus. Apo tōn horiōn, ‘from their borders’, is territorial language.
verses.text: Luke explains the request: the people were seized with great fear (8:37). Matthew ends the whole story here, with the entire town coming out to beg Jesus to leave (8:34), and does not tell what became of the healed men.

verses.context: As Jesus boards the boat, the healed man begs to go with him. Jesus refuses and sends him home to tell his own people what the Lord has done. In Jewish Galilee Jesus often told the healed to keep silent (1:44); here, among Gentiles, he commissions a witness.
verses.grammar: Hina met' autou ē, ‘that he might be with him’, repeats almost exactly the purpose for which Jesus appointed the Twelve in 3:14 (hina ōsin met' autou). The man asks for what the apostles were given, and Jesus gives him a different calling. Ouk aphēken auton, ‘he did not permit him’, answers the permission granted to the demons (verse 13). Hupage eis ton oikon sou pros tous sous, ‘go to your house, to your own’, and apangeilon, ‘report’, are imperatives. Hosa ho kurios soi pepoiēken kai ēleēsen se, ‘how much the Lord has done for you and has had mercy on you’, joins a perfect (what has been done stands) and an aorist (the act of mercy).

theology.note: The first person in Mark sent to proclaim Jesus to Gentiles is a man who a few hours earlier lived among tombs. His commission is not to follow Jesus from place to place but to go home, and the verse gives that kind of witness its own dignity.

verses.context: The man goes further than he was told: not only to his household but throughout the Decapolis, and he proclaims not what "the Lord" had done but what "Jesus" had done. Everyone marvels. When Jesus returns to this region in 7:31, a crowd will bring him a deaf man at once.
verses.grammar: Ērxato kērussein, ‘he began to proclaim’, uses the verb Mark reserves for the proclamation of John (1:4, 7), Jesus (1:14, 38-39), and the Twelve (3:14, 6:12). The man is counted among the proclaimers. The swap from ho kurios in verse 19 to ho Iēsous in verse 20 is quiet but deliberate: what the Lord (God) did, Jesus did. Ethaumazon, an imperfect, ‘they kept marveling’, describes a continuing response.
verses.history: The Decapolis, ‘ten cities’, was a group of Greek cities east of the Jordan (with Scythopolis, Beth-shan, on its west bank) that had been freed from Hasmonean Jewish rule when Pompey organized the region in 63 BC. Pliny the Elder lists them (Natural History 5.74) as Damascus, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Raphana, Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippos, Dion, Pella, Galasa (Gerasa), and Canatha, noting that writers disagreed about the list. They were Greek in language, religion, and civic life, with temples, theaters, and colonnaded streets whose ruins still stand at Jerash and Beth-shan.
verses.text: Luke says the man proclaimed ‘throughout the whole city’ (8:39) and keeps the shift from God to Jesus: ‘how much God had done’ becomes ‘how much Jesus had done’. Matthew omits the man's commission and proclamation entirely.

theology.note: Jesus tells the man to report what ‘the Lord’ has done; the man reports what Jesus has done, and Mark lets both statements stand. The narrative identifies the work of Jesus with the work of Israel's God without comment.

verses.context: Jesus crosses back to the western, Jewish shore, and a crowd gathers again. A synagogue leader named Jairus falls at his feet. After an unnamed Gentile possessed by a legion comes a named, respected Jewish official, and both end up on their knees before Jesus.
verses.grammar: Diaperasantos tou Iēsou, ‘Jesus having crossed over’, is another genitive absolute scene-setter. Heis tōn archisunagōgōn, ‘one of the synagogue rulers’, implies more than one, either in a single synagogue or in the town. Erchetai and piptei, ‘comes’ and ‘falls’, are historic presents. Piptei pros tous podas autou, ‘he falls at his feet’, is the same gesture as the demoniac's (verse 6) and the woman's (verse 33), each time from a different kind of person.
verses.history: An archisunagōgos was the official responsible for a synagogue's services and building, deciding who would read and preach (compare Acts 13:15). The title appears in a Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 and usually dated before AD 70, which records that Theodotus, a priest and archisunagōgos, son and grandson of archisunagōgoi, built a synagogue for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments, with a guest house for travelers from abroad. The post could run in families and carried standing in a town. Jairus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yair (Jair), borne by a son of Manasseh and a judge of Israel (Numbers 32:41, Judges 10:3).
verses.text: Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts omit ‘named Jairus’, probably to bring Mark into line with Matthew, who does not give the name (9:18). The name is firmly attested in the other manuscripts and in Luke (8:41). Matthew calls him simply ‘a ruler’ (archōn).

verses.context: Jairus pleads for his little daughter, who is at the point of death, and asks Jesus to come and lay hands on her. Jesus goes, and the crowd follows, pressing around him. The press of the crowd sets up the next scene, in which one touch among many will be different.
verses.grammar: Parakalei auton polla, ‘he begs him earnestly’, uses the verb of the Gerasene story once more. Thugatrion, ‘little daughter’, is a diminutive, a word of tenderness. Eschatōs echei, literally ‘has it at the last’, is an idiom of everyday Greek meaning ‘is at the point of death’. Hina elthōn epithēs tas cheiras autē, ‘that coming you lay your hands on her’, uses hina with the subjunctive as a polite command, an idiom grammarians call the imperatival hina (‘please come’). The second hina gives the purpose: hina sōthē kai zēsē, ‘that she may be saved and live’. Sōzō here means to be healed, but Mark's readers knew its wider sense of salvation. In verse 24 sunethlibon auton, ‘they were pressing against him’, from thlibō, ‘to squeeze’, prepares for the disciples' objection in verse 31.
verses.text: The Gospels differ over the girl's condition when her father comes. In Mark she is at the point of death and news of her death comes later (verse 35); Luke says she was dying, adds that she was his only daughter and about twelve (8:42), and keeps the messengers (8:49); Matthew, who abbreviates the story, has the father say at the start that she has just died (9:18) and omits the messengers.

theology.note: Jairus asks that his daughter be "healed and live", and Mark uses the verb sōzō, ‘save’. In the Gospels healing of the body and rescue of the whole person share one vocabulary; the story will show Jesus' salvation reaching past sickness into death itself.

verses.context: Mark interrupts the story of Jairus with another, a technique scholars call intercalation or a Markan sandwich: one story is framed by another so that each interprets the other (compare 3:20-35, 6:7-30, 11:12-25, 14:1-11). A woman who has bled for twelve years has spent everything on doctors and grown worse.
verses.grammar: Verses 25 to 27 are one long sentence built from seven participles before the main verb arrives in verse 27: ousa, ‘being’ (with a flow of blood), pathousa, ‘having suffered’, dapanēsasa, ‘having spent’, ōphelētheisa, ‘having been helped’ (with mēden, ‘not at all’), elthousa, ‘having come’ (to worse), akousasa, ‘having heard’, elthousa, ‘having come’, and finally hēpsato, ‘she touched’. The structure makes the reader live through twelve years of loss before the single act of touching. En rhusei haimatos, ‘in a flow of blood’, echoes the language of Leviticus 15:25 in the Septuagint. Polla pathousa hupo pollōn iatrōn, ‘having suffered many things under many physicians’, plays on polla and pollōn.
verses.history: The Mishnah preserves a harsh proverb, that the best of physicians is bound for Gehenna (m. Qiddushin 4:14), and the Babylonian Talmud (b. Shabbat 110a-b) records a string of folk remedies for a woman with a chronic flow of blood, including potions and rituals, which suggests what treatment might have involved. The twelve years matter for more than length: under Leviticus 15:25-27 she was unclean for the whole period, as was anything she lay or sat on. James R. Edwards, in a 1989 study of Mark's ‘sandwiches’, showed how the framing stories illuminate each other; here the woman's twelve years of bleeding and the girl's twelve years of life (verse 42) are set side by side.
verses.text: Luke, traditionally a physician (Colossians 4:14), says only that no one could heal her (8:43), leaving out Mark's remark that the doctors made her worse. Some manuscripts of Luke add that she had spent all her living on physicians, but the earliest (including P75 and Vaticanus) lack it. Matthew abbreviates to the twelve years alone (9:20).

verses.context: Having heard about Jesus, the woman comes up behind him in the crowd and touches his cloak. She acts secretly, as her uncleanness and her shame would require, and her reasoning is simple: if she touches even his clothes, she will be healed.
verses.grammar: Opisthen, ‘from behind’, captures her concealment. Elegen gar hoti, ‘for she was saying’, is an imperfect, ‘she kept saying’, and Matthew adds ‘to herself’ (9:21). Ean hapsōmai kan tōn himatiōn autou, ‘if I touch even his garments’: kan, ‘even’, shows that she thinks touching his clothes is less than touching him, and yet enough. Sōthēsomai, ‘I will be saved’, is a future passive, the same verb as in Jairus's request (verse 23). Haptomai, ‘to touch’, takes the genitive in Greek, as English says ‘take hold of’.
verses.history: Matthew and Luke say she touched the kraspedon of his cloak, the tassel that the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their garments as a reminder of the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39, Deuteronomy 22:12). Mark uses the word later, when crowds beg to touch even the fringe of his cloak (6:56). Belief that power could pass through clothing or even a shadow appears again in Acts (5:15, 19:11-12).

theology.note: Her faith is mixed with what looks like superstition, and it is secret. Jesus neither mocks it nor lets it stay as it is: he will call it faith and then bring her face to face with him. The verses show that faith can be real before it is well understood.

verses.context: The healing is instant and physical. The source of her bleeding dries up, and she knows in her body that she is healed. The Gospel records what the woman felt, not what the crowd saw; for the moment the miracle is hers alone.
verses.grammar: Exēranthē hē pēgē tou haimatos autēs, ‘the fountain of her blood was dried up’: pēgē, ‘spring’ or ‘fountain’, is the word the Septuagint uses in Leviticus 12:7 for the source of a woman's bleeding (Hebrew meqor dameha), so Mark's phrase is the law's own language. Exēranthē is the verb used of the withered seed in 4:6 and the withered hand in 3:1. Egnō tō sōmati, ‘she knew in her body’: the knowledge is bodily. Iatai, a perfect passive, ‘she has been healed’, describes a completed cure that holds. Mastix, ‘affliction’, literally means a whip or scourge.

theology.note: The healing is embodied and immediate, and the woman knows it in her flesh. Scripture's hope is never salvation from the body but of it, and the verse takes a woman's body, which had been the place of her exclusion, as the place of God's mercy.

verses.context: Jesus knows at once that power has gone out from him, turns, and asks who touched his clothes. The disciples think the question absurd in such a crowd, but Jesus keeps looking. The woman wanted healing without meeting; Jesus insists on the meeting.
verses.grammar: Epignous en heautō tēn ex autou dunamin exelthousan, ‘knowing in himself the power from him having gone out’, is compressed Greek: the power is his and it has gone forth. Dunamis is Mark's word for Jesus' mighty works (6:2, 5). The disciples' reply uses sunthlibonta, ‘pressing in’, echoing verse 24. Perieblepeto, an imperfect middle, ‘he kept looking around’, is a Markan word for Jesus' searching gaze (3:5, 34). Idein tēn touto poiēsasan, ‘to see the one who had done this’, uses a feminine participle: Mark's narration already knows it was a woman, while Jesus' question in the story is left open.
verses.text: Luke gives the objection to Peter and has Jesus say he knows power has gone out from him (8:45-46). Matthew omits the search and the disciples' objection: Jesus simply turns, sees her, and speaks (9:22).

theology.note: Did Jesus not know who touched him, or did he ask in order to draw her out? John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew's version (Homilies on Matthew 31), held that he knew and called her forward to free her from fear and to make her faith known. Many modern interpreters take the question at face value, seeing in it the real limits of knowledge the Son accepted in becoming human (compare Mark 13:32). Both readings confess him fully divine and fully human; they differ on how that union showed itself in this moment.

verses.context: The woman comes forward in fear, falls at his feet, and tells the whole truth. Jesus calls her "Daughter", says her faith has made her well, and sends her away in peace. What she had hidden becomes public, and her healing becomes a restoration before the whole crowd.
verses.grammar: Phobētheisa kai tremousa, ‘afraid and trembling’, is the language of someone expecting a rebuke. Eiduia ho gegonen autē, ‘knowing what had happened to her’, uses a perfect (gegonen): the change is complete. Eipen autō pasan tēn alētheian, ‘she told him the whole truth’. Thugatēr, ‘daughter’, is a nominative used as a form of address, and it is the only time in Mark that Jesus calls anyone by that word. Hē pistis sou sesōken se, ‘your faith has saved you’, uses a perfect, a salvation that stands. Hupage eis eirēnēn, ‘go into peace’, reproduces the Hebrew farewell lekhi leshalom (1 Samuel 1:17). Isthi hugiēs, ‘be healthy’, is a present imperative: remain well.
verses.text: Luke adds that she declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him and how she had been healed (8:47), which makes the public restoration explicit. Matthew has Jesus say ‘take courage, daughter’ and dates the healing ‘from that hour’ (9:22), so that in Matthew the healing follows Jesus' word rather than the touch.

theology.note: Jesus credits her faith, not the cloak. Faith is not a power that heals but trust that reaches for Jesus, and by drawing her forward he turns a touch of his clothes into a meeting with him.

"Your faith has healed you" uses the same verb as "saved", and the healing is followed by peace and a new name, daughter. Her salvation includes her body, her place among God's people, and her relation to Jesus.

verses.context: While Jesus is still speaking, messengers arrive from Jairus's house: the girl is dead, and there is no reason to trouble the Teacher further. The delay caused by the woman has, it seems, cost the girl her life. Jesus speaks to Jairus before he can despair: do not fear, only believe.
verses.grammar: Eti autou lalountos, ‘while he was still speaking’, is a genitive absolute that ties the two stories together in time. Apethanen, an aorist, ‘she died’, states it flatly. Ti eti skulleis ton didaskalon, ‘why still trouble the Teacher?’: skullō first meant to flay or mangle and came to mean to harass or bother. Parakousas can mean ‘overhearing’ or ‘ignoring’; in the Septuagint and in Matthew 18:17 it means to refuse to listen, and many commentators think Mark means that Jesus heard the report and disregarded it. Mē phobou, monon pisteue, ‘do not fear, only believe’, are two present imperatives. A present imperative with mē is often read as ‘stop being afraid’, though grammarians caution that the form does not always carry that sense; the second, pisteue, is a call to go on trusting.
verses.text: Luke expands the command: ‘do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed’ (8:50). Matthew has no messengers, since in his version the girl was already dead when her father came (9:18).

theology.note: Faith is asked for exactly when circumstances make it seem pointless. Jesus sets fear and faith against each other again, as after the storm (4:40), and asks Jairus to keep trusting past the report of death.

verses.context: Jesus limits his company to Peter, James, and John. This is the first time Mark singles out the three, who will be with Jesus again at the transfiguration (9:2) and in Gethsemane (14:33); each time they witness something of who Jesus is that the others do not see.
verses.grammar: Ouk aphēken oudena met' autou sunakolouthēsai ei mē, ‘he did not allow anyone to follow along with him except’, uses a double negative for emphasis and then the exception. In Greek a single article governs all three names (ton Petron kai Iakōbon kai Iōannēn), presenting them as one group. Iōannēn ton adelphon Iakōbou, ‘John the brother of James’, identifies John by his brother, as in 3:17.
verses.text: Luke names the three at the door of the house, together with the girl's parents (8:51), and puts John before James, as he sometimes does (Luke 9:28, Acts 1:13). Matthew does not mention the three.

verses.context: At the house the mourning has begun: noise, weeping, loud wailing. Jesus says the child is not dead but asleep, and they laugh at him. He puts them all out and takes only the parents and his three disciples into the room where the child lies.
verses.grammar: Theōrei thorubon, ‘he sees an uproar’, is a historic present. Alalazontas, ‘wailing’, is an onomatopoeic word from the ritual cry of mourning (compare the Hebrew wail in Jeremiah 4:8). Jesus' question, ti thorubeisthe kai klaiete, ‘why are you making an uproar and weeping?’, turns their noise back on them. To paidion ouk apethanen alla katheudei, ‘the child did not die but is sleeping’, sets an aorist for death against a present for sleep. Kategelōn autou, ‘they were laughing him down’, is an imperfect of scornful laughter. Autos de ekbalōn pantas, ‘but he, throwing them all out’: ekballō is the verb Mark uses for casting out demons (1:34, 39), and the same force is turned on the mourners.
verses.history: The Mishnah rules that even the poorest man in Israel must provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (m. Ketubbot 4:4), which shows that professional mourning was expected at every death. Matthew mentions the flute players (9:23). Luke adds that they laughed because they knew she was dead (8:53), which rules out the suggestion that she was merely in a coma.

ot.note: Daniel's vision of the end says that many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame. The Hebrew calls the dead yeshenei, ‘sleepers’, and the Greek versions render it with katheudō, the verb Jesus uses here. Jesus' ‘not dead but sleeping’ does not deny the death; it names it in the language of resurrection hope. Paul uses the same image for believers who have died (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14), and John records Jesus saying Lazarus has fallen asleep before stating plainly that he is dead (John 11:11-14).

theology.note: Jesus calls death sleep, as Scripture does when it speaks of the dead who will be raised. The laughter of the mourners is the world's verdict that death is final; Jesus' word is the verdict of the one who will overturn it.

verses.context: Jesus takes the dead girl by the hand and speaks two Aramaic words, which Mark keeps and translates. She rises at once and walks around. Only now does Mark give her age: twelve, the same number as the woman's years of suffering.
verses.grammar: Kratēsas tēs cheiros tou paidiou, ‘grasping the child's hand’, is the gesture with which Jesus raised Peter's mother-in-law (1:31). Touching a corpse made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11), but here, as with the woman, the direction is reversed: life flows from Jesus rather than uncleanness to him. Talitha koum is Aramaic, ṭalyetha qum, ‘little girl, get up’. Mark translates it with korasion, a diminutive, ‘little girl’, and adds soi legō, ‘I say to you’, which is not in the Aramaic but brings out the note of command. Egeire, ‘rise’, is the verb used of Jesus' own resurrection (16:6). Anestē, ‘she arose’, is from anistēmi, the other resurrection verb (8:31). Periepatei, an imperfect, ‘she began walking around’. Exestēsan ekstasei megalē, ‘they were amazed with great amazement’, is a cognate dative, another Semitic way of intensifying, like the ‘great fear’ of 4:41.
verses.text: The earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others) read koum, the masculine form of the Aramaic imperative; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version (‘cumi’), read koumi, the correct feminine form for a girl. The shorter form is the harder reading and probably original; spoken Aramaic in Galilee may have used the masculine form for both. Mark preserves Jesus' Aramaic in several other places (3:17, 7:34, 14:36, 15:34). Luke omits the Aramaic and adds that her spirit returned (8:55); Matthew says only that Jesus took her hand and she arose (9:25).

ot.note: Elijah raised the widow's son at Zarephath by stretching himself on the boy three times and crying to the LORD, and the Hebrew says the child's life (nefesh) returned to him. Elisha raised the Shunammite's son after shutting the door and praying, then lying on the child twice (2 Kings 4:32-35). Both prophets pray and labor. Jesus takes the girl's hand and speaks two words. Luke, who knows the Elijah story well (Luke 4:25-26, 7:11-16), adds that her spirit returned (8:55), which recalls the Hebrew of 1 Kings 17:22 (the Septuagint there says instead that the child cried out).

theology.note: This is the first raising of the dead in Mark. The girl returns to ordinary mortal life and will die again, so it is a sign rather than the resurrection itself, but Mark describes it with the two verbs he will use for Jesus' own rising, and it points to the one who will conquer death for good.

verses.context: Jesus gives strict orders that no one should know, and tells them to give the girl something to eat. The command to silence seems impossible to keep with mourners outside; the command to feed her is the most ordinary thing in the story, and the most tender.
verses.grammar: Diesteilato autois polla, ‘he ordered them strictly’, uses the same polla as an adverb that marked Jairus's begging (verse 23). Hina mēdeis gnoi touto, ‘that no one should know this’, uses a rare subjunctive form (gnoi). Eipen dothēnai autē phagein, ‘he said that something be given her to eat’, uses a passive infinitive: the parents are to do it.
verses.history: Jesus' repeated commands to silence (1:34, 1:44, 3:12, 7:36, 8:30, 9:9) were made famous by William Wrede's The Messianic Secret in the Gospels (1901), which argued that the theme was Mark's own device to explain why Jesus had not been recognized as Messiah in his lifetime. Later scholars have offered other explanations: that Jesus avoided the political expectations attached to the title Messiah, that he wanted to be known through the cross rather than the miracles (9:9), or that the secrecy was a real feature of his ministry that Mark developed. Matthew, who omits the command, says instead that the news spread through all that region (9:26).

theology.note: Feeding the girl proves she is truly alive in the body, as the risen Jesus will later eat before his disciples (Luke 24:41-43). The bodily reality of the raising is part of its meaning.
